samples.question: The picture shows a wiring harness on white paper. Grey wires of equal thickness join only where they meet at a junction, and no two wires cross anywhere in the picture, so wires that merely pass near each other are not joined. Three junctions are marked by round coloured patches - one red, one green, one blue - and the grey wires are painted across these patches, so the wiring runs through each patch without a break. Now imagine rubbing out one whole round patch: everything inside that circle disappears, including the pieces of grey wire crossing it, while all ink outside the circle stays exactly as drawn, including the other two patches and their wiring. The remaining grey wiring is in one piece if you can travel between any two bits of grey wire along grey wire the whole way, never jumping a gap. As drawn, before any rubbing out, all the grey wiring is a single piece. Rubbing out exactly one of the three patches breaks the remaining grey wiring into two or more separate pieces; rubbing out either of the other two leaves it in one piece. Which patch is the one that breaks the wiring? Answer 'red', 'green', or 'blue'.
